title: Book 14 opens: churchgoers must be washed of sin’s stain
english: ON ADORATION AND WORSHIP IN SPIRIT AND TRUTH — BOOK FOURTEEN. That those willing to frequent in churches must be clean and washed-out as to the stain from sin, and thus stand beside God.

Cyril: So then concerning the tent and indeed also concerning priests and Levitical under-service these things seem to me to have been said most sufficiently, and I think to have been examined finely. Fit
translator_notes: Ends mid Πρέ into §2 ποι; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Ascend Lord’s house clean; eject leper/flux/soul-unclean from camp
english: Cyril: …ting would be most of all for those who would choose to live rightly, and the altogether well-fitting of the citizenship in Christ, as a kind of crown to bind upon their own heads, to urge one another headlong as it were saying: ‘Come, and let us go up unto the mountain of Lord, and unto the house of the God of Jacob, and he will announce to us his way, and we will walk in it;’ when also some having received the thus well-famed and benefit-bearing voice, all but also leap up saying: ‘I was gladdened upon those having said to me: Unto a house of Lord we will go.’ So then, O Palladius, for those hastening to go unto a house of God, of what sort would the aim be and the mind for them wherever then it would look, and what longing to set upright, they go unto the sacred and divine tent?
Palladius: And indeed, O companion, the matter is not unclear; for it has been written, that ‘Worship the Lord in his holy court;’ and ‘Lift sacrifices, and go into his courts.’

Cyril: So then bringing forward the sacrifices over themselves, clear that the spiritual ones, and indeed also about to approach according to intelligible worship, some go into the house of Lord and into his courts.
Palladius: Thus I say.

Cyril: So then shall we think those willing to frequent-in, must dart through simply, not having been washed-out as to the sin, not having been freed from abomination, not having been scraped-off as it were of the filth of flesh-love, but having the mind melted-in, and having a rusted heart? Least at least, but rather having been brightened with the brightness in Christ, and gleaming-through the all-variegated beauty of the most God-loving virtue.
Palladius: Very much so; for I at least say one must go according to eyes of Lord, with every stain of our thoughts having been rubbed-out beforehand.

Cyril: You spoke rightly, since at least he also makes the sick one hated, and indeed also rejectable, and sends out from the multitude of the holy ones. Which also the all-divine Paul writing understands very well: ‘So then lift out the evil one from yourselves.’ And I would not say the matter a fruit of wildness of customs, but a wise finding of safety. ‘For a little leaven,’ he says, ‘leavens the whole lump.’ This again also a sacred law was under-forming for us riddlingly. For it has been written in the Numbers: ‘And the Lord spoke toward Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and let them send out from the camp every leper and every flux-flowing, and every unclean upon soul, from male unto female, send out outside the camp, and they will not defile their camps in which I lodge in them. And the sons of Israel did thus.’ So then is it not true to say that very hard-to-bear and truly hard-to-carry is the burden of the law? For you understand how also upon unwilling sicknesses he writes-down a judgment, and yet
translator_notes: Ends mid καίτοι into §3 κατοικτείρεσθαι; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Bodily ills type spiritual; leper = flesh works; flux begins
english: Cyril: …one must pity those having fallen into such misfortunes; for in return for what then would someone puzzle also very reasonably, that he was making the leper houseless and sendable-away, and indeed toward these also the one held-down by a passion of flux-flow, and again the unclean upon soul?
Palladius: I would not have to understand, and you yourself would perhaps speak.

Cyril: So then I think that of the things in thickness and bodily matters there was not a very great word beside God, for the one pre-forming for us the divine and spiritual worship. For the things outside law are punished, and as many as appear having stepped out of the fitting, these I would say are under judgment and justice, but a bodily sickness would in no manner strike against the laws. So then it will lie reasonably also farthest from a writing, and the being charged toward someone it would not have from anywhere; or is it not clear for everyone, that no one is sick willingly, and everyone then, I think, makes being well-strong most wishable?
Palladius: Truly.

Cyril: So then even if the word should have something unbeautiful of the history, the grieving is nothing, if the spiritual things should be led through well toward at least what seems good to the lawgiver. So then leprosy is a dying of flesh, and the passion most devouring. Therefore also the all-divine Moses, with Miriam having been leproused for him, having become fearful, and very cheerless, was entreating, saying: ‘O God, I beg you, heal her,’ for he said: ‘Let her not become as a miscarriage going out from a mother’s womb, and it will eat down the half of her fleshes.’ And a flux-flowing, what would I say, of what sort the passion? for no one has been ignorant. And at least that some are unclean upon soul, signals some such thing: the touching a departed one and becoming near a dead body, the law was reckoning for the more ancient ones unto a manner of defilement, showing the deadness hated to God the one able to make-alive all things. And indeed also otherwise, receiving the matter unto a dying of mind and soul as in a thick type. And a dead and cooled-out mind, the sin-loving, and accustomed to be without-share of the manly-acts unto life. But if it happened for some to have died, somehow every necessity, for those own from blood and according to race to understand and to do upon him the things having been customed; yet unclean also these according to the law, and not altogether and unto all, but there was for them some manner of cleansing-back. You have a sufficient clarifying of the history.
Palladius: And very much.

Cyril: So then come, transforming it unto spiritual contemplation, let us say that: that the leper signals for us the one having been spotted with varied passions unto youthfulness. And these are the works of the flesh, which also the most wise Paul himself was numbering for us saying: ‘Fornication, uncleanness, idolatry, enmities, strife, angers, jealousies.’ And another at least,
translator_notes: Ends mid Ἕτερός γε μὴν into §4 τοῦτ' ἔστιν ὁ γονοῤῥυής; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Flux = wasted fertility; soul-unclean = share others’ deadness; crushed/cut begin
english: Cyril: …that is, the flux-flowing, the one always and unrestrainedly in defilements, and spending the fitness of the nature toward virtuous and admirable fruit-bearing unto nothing.
Palladius: And of what sort do you say?

Cyril: Broad very much is the word upon all; and for now I will use one clear and most vivid example, toward proof of what I said: those having a well-natured mind and as it were somehow scraped-off, putting it into the words about the truth, will they not have the well-fitting in rightness and exactness of doctrines as a fruit not unadmirable?
Palladius: And very much.

Cyril: And those at least having chosen not to think and do this, but rather turning aside from the necessary way, and setting up an advocate of unholy doctrines, or showing a helper of the wickedness in world, make a begetter of deceit and deception, damaging for nothing useful the fitness of the nature toward the good, and they write-down for us very well the flux-flowing, and show a soul-weakness same-natured with a bodily passion in own manners.
Palladius: You spoke rightly.

Cyril: And the unclean upon soul somehow altogether signals the one having shared of others’ deadness, and being filled lazily with alien faults, toward whom also the divine David somehow said: ‘If you were seeing a thief, you were running-with him, and with an adulterer you were setting your portion.’ For just as doing what is not lawful damages and deadens soul and mind, so also consenting with those doing them, and the one willing-with would also be a sharer with those self-working unto sin. For he is not somehow unchargeable. Therefore also Paul: ‘Keep yourself pure,’ he says, ‘and do not share alien sins;’ this, I think, is the being defiled upon a dead one intelligibly.
Palladius: It seems so.

Cyril: So then he has ordered very well the leper and flux-flowing and unclean upon the soul to depart from the synagogue, not allowing those having the hard-to-wash-out uncleanness to be woven-up with the choruses of the holy ones? ‘For what sharing of light toward darkness? or what portion for a faithful with an unfaithful?’ he says.
Palladius: So then slippery, the going as with unwashed feet into a house of God.

Cyril: Most slippery indeed, if at least it is true that striking against God is not without-damage. And he also shuts out others from the holy court in Deuteronomy, saying: ‘A crushed one and a cut-off one will not go into a church of Lord, one from a whore will not go into a church of Lord; an Ammonite and a Moabite will not go into a church of Lord, and unto a tenth generation will not go into a church of Lord, and unto the age, because of the not’
translator_notes: Ends mid παρὰ τὸ μὴ into §5 συναντῆσαι; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Crushed vs cut manhood type; Ammon=heretics; Moab=idolaters
english: Cyril: …meeting them for you with breads and water in the way, with you going out from Egypt, and that they hired against you Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia to curse you. And Lord your God did not wish to hearken to Balaam, and Lord your God turned the curses into a blessing, because Lord your God loved you. You will not address peaceful things to them, and beneficial things for them, all your days unto the age.’
Palladius: And who would be understood crushed and cut-off, Ammonite and Moabite, I would wish to learn thoroughly.

Cyril: Hear then; the of the making of eunuchs is not one manner, not one, O Palladius, but some double is said to be, and has been found-out. For some are cutters and having been torn-apart as to the male things; and others still bear crushed and altogether useless things, and some sometimes cut-off rawly and unholily the child-making part of the body, and are inactive toward the of a man, and yet finishing among men by nature and age; and a symbol of manliness, the male things. So then one must suspect the crushed, the as it were somehow not having been pulled-out altogether as to soul and mind, but rather somehow saving in himself the shattered manliness upon goods, and indeed the cut-off, the one having thrown them away wholly, and having been deprived of the things most fitting for men. And in equal as it were a charge, with the not wishing to man-up at all, the loving not to man-up healthily.
Palladius: Of what sort then do you say?

Cyril: Some have fallen-back into fleshly desires, having released as it were whole reins to the passion, throwing-beside the mind rotten and unmanly to the pleasures unto wantonness. And others again wonder at continence, and sometimes touch the bright attempts unto this, but fear-out the standing-against, and not bearing the assault of the pleasure, they nod-down toward the strengthless. So then, will you not reasonably call the one having altogether given-up the attempts unto manliness cut-off? And the one having in mind the wishing to man-up, yet not still also being strong to set upright the virtue, will you think crushed, reshaping urbanely also the passions of the body unto a quality of manners, and receiving the in sense as an image of the intelligible and more unapparent?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: And with these was being shut-out-together both Ammonite and Moabite, as unholy and most abominable, and springing-upon the holy ones as lions, and pouring upon those accustomed to be well-reputed the arrows from envy and malice. And they would be a type, Ammonites at least, of the unpitiful heretics. And Moabites again, of those still in the idolatrous wanderings, and having been underlaid with the wickednesses of the demons; for both God-hated, and as it were sick with a brother boldness against the holy ones.
translator_notes: Book 14 §§1–10; PG mid-cuts kept.

title: Ammon/Edom refuse bread; heretics kin who will not help
english: Palladius: I do not very much understand what you say.

Cyril: You understand very well, and not unto long. For Ammonites having become of Esau, were near-sown and same-blooded to the sons from Jacob, I say to Israel; but also somehow neglecting the nature itself, those from Esau were falsifying the manner of kinship, and fearful and unbending were thereafter bearing-down toward those near and from blood, that is of the Israel. For when departing from the of Egyptians he was running-past the land of the Ammonites, he was entreating the dweller as a brother to let-pass, or for them to dart-through and to pity those having been wronged; and he was not releasing. And what do I say this? Rather even in arms, or also he lifts a war. And he would have wronged terribly, if not according to a divine voice, Israel has bent-away; and the having-been-written holds thus: ‘And Moses sent messengers from Kadesh toward a king of Edom, saying: Thus says your brother Israel: You know all the labor having found us. And our fathers went down into Egypt, and we sojourned in Egypt more days, and the Egyptians mistreated us and our fathers. And we cried up toward Lord, and Lord hearkened to our voice, and having sent messengers, led us out from Egypt. And now we are in Kadesh city, from a part of your borders. We will go past through your land. We will not go through through fields, nor through vineyards, nor will we drink water from your pits. By a royal way we will walk; we will not turn aside right nor left, until we should go past your borders. And Edom said toward him: You will not go through through me. And if not, in war I will go out unto a meeting for you.’ And after other things: ‘And Edom went out unto a meeting for him in a heavy crowd, and in a strong hand. And Edom did not wish to give to Israel to go past through his borders. And Israel turned aside from him.’ So then is the word thereafter not clear and vivid?
Palladius: Not somehow very much.

Cyril: For you do not understand that having been joined to those from Israel by a relation according to near-kinship, unloving and hard, and having differed nothing from wild beasts, they were being convicted from the matters themselves? For needing to pity as brothers, being in sweats and labors, they go out having devastated. Therefore the law says: ‘They will not go into a church of Lord, because of their not meeting you with bread and water, with you going out from Egypt,’ that is, through the very unsympathetic, and having gone out from wild ones unto unholiness of manners. And you may see that such toward us the ones having chosen to walk-straight are the peoples and leaders of the heretics. For as far as it came unto at least knowing one and only God the Father, and accepting the faith unto Son and the Spirit, even if they do not have altogether healthily an untrue opinion of the brotherhood toward us, and they bear-bastard the kin by judgment, yet for those being in persecutions they do not help, but rather also
translator_notes: Ends mid μᾶλλον δὲ καὶ into §7 ταῖς παρὰ σφῶν; PG mid-cut kept. Cyril conflates Ammon/Edom in typology—render Greek as written.

title: Heretic workshops like Ammon; Moab=Hellenes; no greeting
english: Cyril: …they load-on with the wickednesses from themselves. ‘For from us they went out, but they were not from us,’ according to the having-been-written. ‘For if they were from us, they would have remained with us.’ To whom also the Savior himself, having the fairness plastered-on, yet not still also accustomed to do the things unto his glory, would address also very reasonably: ‘The one not being with me, is against me, and the one not gathering with me, scatters.’ So then do the God-hated workshops of the heretics seem to you to resemble Ammonites, having been sickly extraordinarily as to the unsympathetic and un-God-loving?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: And observe also Moabites, if it seems good, being most warlike openly for those willing to serve God the only both by nature and truly. For they were worshipers of idols, having taken heart exceptionally in divinations and sorceries, and having been fluttered not moderately about flights of birds, and grinding the teeth at the good-doings of Israel, they were hiring Balaam, and preparing him to curse, and by the unspeakable power of God, the mouth of the diviner was being reshaped toward blessings unwilling for them. Such would be the war of Hellenes against us, begrudging the glory of our Savior, and raising-up against us every strength of the devil, which the divine and from-above grace shakes-down, pouring the strengthless of the herd of the demons, and setting-up the manner of the plot toward the knowing to gladden.
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: And for Ammonites and indeed also for Moabites, untrodden are the holy things and very reasonably; for for whom the daring things are brother and the boldness same-formed, for these it would be fitting also to spring into the equal-balanced justices. And observe at least the firm of the law; for he removes the holy ones of them altogether, and not even so much as to say he wants to go unto common-speech, he enjoins saying: ‘You will not address peaceful things to them, and beneficial things for them you will not speak, all your days unto the age.’ So then is this not vividly, what also a pair of holy ones has taught us out, both Paul and John? For the one was saying: ‘If someone comes toward you, and does not bear this teaching, do not say rejoice to this one,’ and this, I think, is the, ‘You will not address peaceful things to them, and beneficial things for them.’ And the other again, ‘A heretical human after one and a second admonition, refuse, knowing that such a one has been twisted-out.’ This is the, You will not speak beneficial things for them. For the law says one must yield to those very twisted-out, as to mad ones, saying: ‘Walk by the light of your fire, and by the flame which you kindled.’ But the Ammonite is shut out unto a third generation, and a Moabite even until a tenth, from at least the time, as I think, with God under-showing for us the greatness of the indignation upon both. For lesser, according to the likely, is the justice of heretics; one might say
translator_notes: Ends mid φαίη into §8 γὰρ ἄν τις; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Zeal without knowledge; no covenant with nations; Dinah begins
english: Cyril: …for someone also upon them just as of course also upon the Jews. ‘For I witness for them, that they have a zeal of God, but not according to recognition.’ For thinking to be right-speaking and wise, the wretched ones have escaped themselves, and fighting the doctrines of the truth, and having been overpowered by a molded zeal, they think to speak-with for the glory of God, arraying against those walking-straight. And Moabites at least, that is, the bands of Hellenes, nakedly and openly, and without all holding-back, fight the divine glory. Therefore somehow the law has hung a more burdensome justice for them. Yet both are sendable-away from the sacred enclosures, as profane and God-hated.
Palladius: So then a matter not without-damage, as far as it came unto defilements, the loving to go even at least unto words with some alien and other-minded ones.

Cyril: You understand very well. Therefore also the law walls-off those having been washed-out and clean, and already own to God, from their abomination saying: ‘And it will be in the Lord your God’s leading you into the land into which you go there to inherit it, and you will lift out great and many and strong nations from your face, the Hittite, and the Girgashite, and the Amorite, and the Canaanite, and the Perizzite, and the Hivite, and the Jebusite, seven nations many, and great, and stronger than you, and Lord your God will give them over into your hands, and you will strike them, with an obliteration you will obliterate them. You will not covenant a covenant toward them, nor will you pity them, nor will you marry toward them. Your daughter you will not give to his son, and his daughter you will not take for your son, for he will stand-off your son from me, and he will serve other gods.’ So then firm is the law. ‘For you will not set,’ he says, ‘a covenant toward them;’ for uncombinable and unjoinable for the having-been-sanctified, the still profane, for the having-been-lit, the in mist and dark, for the having-been-received-in the unacceptable; for the one going-in toward a sacred and divine tent, the one being thrust out of this.
Palladius: Then what the forethought of the law? and for the sake of what does it also altogether stand-apart the clean from the profane, even if someone should become in a beauty of the virtue?

Cyril: For very much indeed is the fear, O friend; lest somehow also what seems to have stood rightly should receive-in a shaking upon what is not fitting and be carried-aside from the proper, having been forced somehow by someone, either of a pleasure stirring, or of the inclination being in the nature thrusting-down unto the fault. For somehow it has always bent-away upon the worthless, and a divine word witnesses for us; ‘For carefully lies,’ he says, ‘the mind of the human upon the evil things from youth.’ And I would set beside for you willing unto a vivid proof, as many things as a word says the from Jacob endured.
Palladius: Dinah somehow you say; for I think thus.
Cyril: Very much so, O Palladius; for it has been written thus in the book of the Genesis: ‘And there came’
translator_notes: Ends mid Καὶ ἦλθεν into §9 Ἰακὼβ εἰς Σαλὴμ; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Dinah leaves tent; soul ruined by alien daughters; David’s one ask
english: Cyril: …Jacob unto Salem city of Shechem, which is in land Canaan, when he returned from Mesopotamia of Syria, and he encamped opposite face of the city, and he acquired the portion of the field, where he set there his tent, from Hamor father of Shechem, for a hundred lambs, and he set there an altar, and he called-upon the God of Israel. And Dinah went out, the daughter of Leah, whom she bore for Jacob, to learn thoroughly the daughters of the locals, and Shechem the son of Hamor the Hivite, the ruler of the land, saw her. And having taken her, he lay with her. And he humbled her. And he held toward the soul of Dinah the daughter of Jacob. And he loved the virgin, and he spoke according to the mind of the virgin to her.’ So then observe that still loving-to-be and lodging in the tent of the father, in which also he called-upon the God of Israel, and a reverend altar had been raised, she was still unprofane and in the boasts of the virginity. And when she ran out of the paternal tent, and having left the sacred space, was being mixed with alien women, she was being forced at once toward uncustomary profanation, and was no longer a virgin, having been borne under unwillingly at the beginnings by the pleasures of others, and having suffered after this also the wishing to be with the one having overreached. ‘For he spoke,’ he says, ‘according to the mind of the virgin to her.’
Palladius: Thus it holds.

Cyril: So then setting beside the sense-perceptible unto an image of the intelligible, come then let us say, that a soul dwelling as it were some exceptional citizenship as a tent, will be all-holy and clean, and having been freed from every abomination, and if it should go out somewhere, and hasten toward the daughters of the alien-tribes, that is, if it should seek-out and spy the life of those in world, the well-natured and well-born mind will be corrupted; for it would not be without-damage for those for whom the aim would become, the living-through brightly, to live-with the worthless. But the divine David at least was not being caught wishing to go outside the sacred tent, but rather to love-to-be and dwell not far, he was making of the things most through prayer saying: ‘One thing I asked from Lord, this I will seek, the dwelling me in a house of Lord all the days of my life, to look-at the delightfulness of Lord, and to visit his holy temple. Because he hid me in his tent in a day of my evils, he sheltered me in a hidden of his tent.’ A tent, I think, saying the divine and sacred, as at least in these, the firm and unshakeable of the pure citizenship, upon which somehow also having gone-in, he was untakeable for those of the passions wishing to devastate.
Palladius: It seems so.

Cyril: And what? would someone not learn more clearly and more truly, that the sharings toward alien-born would somehow produce things beyond every defilement even for those having been trusted to have been fixed, having brought-beside
translator_notes: Ends mid παρενεγκὼν into §10 εἰς ἀπόδειξιν Σολομῶντος; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Solomon’s foreign wives; pleasure dethrones wisdom; no whore in Israel
english: Cyril: …unto a proof the finishing of Solomon’s life, and what things it happened for him to suffer, upon him on a threshold of old-age?
Palladius: How did you speak?

Cyril: For he was thus bright and sung-of, so as somehow already to take the incomparable glory, yet he changed-over unto the unbeautiful, rather even he leaped-down ignobly, unto somehow the last of the impiety unto God. And the things upon him hold thus. For it has been written in the third of the Kingdoms: ‘And Solomon was magnified over all the kings of the earth in wealth and prudence. And all the kings of the earth were seeking the face of Solomon, to hear his prudence, which Lord gave in his heart.’ But the thus well-famed and sung-of, and having driven through unto this of wisdom thereafter, so as to become in unmeasured wonder, and beside those very distinguished, a pleasure of evil women levered-out, and as it were somehow taking him out of the divine tent itself put him into the pits of the idolatry. For it has been written thus about him: ‘And the king Solomon was woman-loving, and he took alien women, and the daughter of Pharaoh; Moabitesses, and Ammonitesses, and Idumaeans, Syrians, Hittites, Amorites, from the nations, which Lord forbade for the sons of Israel: You will not go in toward them, and they themselves will not go in toward you, in order that they may not turn aside your hearts behind their idols. Unto them Solomon was glued, to love. And there were for him ruling women seven hundred, and concubines three hundred. And it became in the time of Solomon’s old-age, and the alien women turned aside his heart behind other gods. And his heart was not complete with Lord his God, just as the heart of David his father. And Solomon walked behind the Astarte abomination of Sidonians, and behind their king idol of sons of Ammon; and Solomon did evil before Lord, and he did not walk behind Lord, as David his father.’ So then is it not worthy to wail for the one said to have suffered such? The one having raised that well-famed temple in the Jerusalems, the one having asked the wisdom sitting-beside the divine thrones, the one having been wondered-at upon the incomparable understanding, and unto the ends themselves of the under heaven, the one as a morning-star, apparent for cities and lands, being worsted by shameful women, and going behind a most polluted pleasure, is caught having fallen unto this of folly, so as also to neglect altogether the piety unto God. So then slippery then and undebatably is the being with the alien-tribes according to the same. And altogether most terrible also the being worsted by the fleshly pleasure, and unclean such a one, and having been hated by the all-holy God, and not without virtue, to drive into the sacred and divine tent. But neither would he bring forward an acceptable sacrifice. For it has been written in Deuteronomy: ‘There will not be a whore from daughters of Israel, and there will not be a whoring one from sons of Israel; and there will not be’
translator_notes: Ends mid καὶ οὐκ ἔσται into later §§; tip §§1–10.

title: No whore’s wage or dog’s exchange on altar; forced vs willing impurity
english: Cyril: …bringing-to-end from daughters of Israel, and there will not be a being-brought-to-end from sons of Israel; you will not bring forward a hire of a whore, nor an exchange of a dog into the house of Lord your God toward every vow, because an abomination to Lord your God is even both.’
Palladius: How sharp the law, and of the most beneficial things as much as most!

Cyril: Well done, O Palladius; for you understand rightly. For you would be struck-down, I think, and still more greatly, having thought-through that checking very well the smooth unto pleasures, he sends-away the wanton and unchastened. For see how both for those willing to practice voluntary and self-chosen the defilement upon shamefulness, and indeed also for those accustomed to bring-down others unto this as from necessity, he is seen laying-on, and through the things he denies the needing to do, he finishes them safer, and constructs for them hard-to-find the word able to suffice for defenses. For no longer are the charges of ignorance, but thereafter of easiness and of an unsubmissive mind the writing.
Palladius: How did you speak?
Cyril: For do not some go self-called unto the whoring, and women and youths willing to wage-earn, sell-down the bloom to some men’s unrestraint?
Palladius: Yes.

Cyril: And what? are not some worsted by shameful gains, and having put-forward to those willing their own maidservants, or of the males, whom they might somehow buy-out, the wretched ones silver-collect? about whom also the prophet says: ‘And the girls they were selling instead of wine, and they were drinking.’ For true that unto this measure of worthlessness and uncleanness some arrive, so as to dare unholily to tribute-collect sometimes even such of the shameful things.
Palladius: I understand.

Cyril: So then they whore willingly, some, the themselves being borne outside the evil, then going unto this by own-judgment; and bringing-to-end at least would be those paying tributes as from necessity to others, and collecting the wages from the wantonness for those having bought.
Palladius: You spoke rightly.

Cyril: So then the law denies the matter everywhere, and makes unholy the one having been caught by a writing, and shuts outside sacred tents, and at once shows the divine altar unapproachable for him, saying the sacrifice will be unacceptable, and the vow unreceivable. For true, that not pure are vows from a hire of a whore. And in equal manner he makes hated and most abominable also the exchange of the dog; and a dog, I think, he says, the easy unto uncleanness, and simply lying-on for those approaching; and an exchange of a dog, the somehow being brought forward for him over him. So then let the law cry-upon: ‘There will not be a whore from daughters of Israel, and there will not be a whoring one from sons of Israel.’ And let the most wise Paul sound-with crying: ‘Flee’
translator_notes: Ends mid Φεύγετε into §12 τὴν πορνείαν; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Flee fornication; living sacrifice; Peor; example opposite the sun
english: Cyril: …the fornication; Every sin which if a human should do is outside the body; and the one whoring sins unto his own body.’ So then let him also call toward the needing to desire the better things those leaping-upon bravely with boasts of continence. For he said again: ‘For I entreat you, brothers, through the compassions of God, present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, well-pleasing to God, your rational worship; and do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, unto your approving what the will of God is, the good and well-pleasing and perfect.’ Or do you not say there is a sacrifice truly holy and all-pure truly, the putting-away of the more shameful things?
Palladius: I at least would say; for how not?

Cyril: And with us departing from fleshly pleasure God is gladdened-upon, and he is very gloomy for those turning-aside toward the strengthless, and for those having chosen to fall behind flesh he brings-on the justices; for hot and unchastened pleasure sometimes even forces unto a standing-away from God. And true that the matter is, the word upon Solomon would show-out at once. And before him Israel having been carried-aside unto this in the desert is caught; for it has been written that ‘Israel lodged in Shittim, and the people was profaned to whore-out unto the daughters of Moab; and they called them unto the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices, and they worshiped their idols, and Israel was finished for Baal-peor, and Lord was angered with wrath for Israel. And Lord said to Moses: Take all the leaders of the people and make-examples of them for Lord opposite the sun, and the wrath of Lord’s wrath will be turned-back from Israel.’ Do you see that somehow the divine and most gentle nature is sharpened, and all but also is carried-out unto unwilling angers toward us? For cattle-fitting is the matter, the raging-upon, I say, the seasons of women, and altogether unholy, and daring to make the unchastened pleasure an exchange of the piety unto God. Therefore also they are made-examples for the Lord opposite the sun, that is, they have been hung from upright woods turned toward east, and this was for them the manner of the punishment, with the type all but having cried-through vividly and releasing a voice, that the all-seeing and unarguable eye of the judging one no one would outrun, having been caught in such stumblings, nor would he go unpaid, but he will lie according to the prophet’s voice unto a seeing for all flesh, holding-under bitter justices of the things having been faulted by him.
Palladius: So then the being punished manifestly, and the as it were somehow having been made-example in eyes of God he says, opposite the sun.

Cyril: Very much so; and the word for us is not from aim; and that for those whoring, or for those having been whored, the words of the thus cold and profane life toward God, and manifest are the hidden things,
translator_notes: Ends mid κεκρυμμένα into §13 γνωσθήσεται; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Numbers jealousy ordeal water quoted in full
english: Cyril: …will be known, and the in each clearly, and through another law again he was typing-through for us. For it has been written in the Numbers: ‘And Lord spoke toward Moses, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, and you will say toward them: Of a man if his woman should transgress, and having overlooked she should overlook him, and someone should sleep with her a bed of seed, and it should escape from eyes of her man, and she should hide, and she herself should be defiled, and a witness was not with her, and she herself should not have been caught, and a spirit of jealousy should come-upon him, and he should be jealous of his woman, and she herself has been defiled, or a spirit of jealousy should come-upon him, and he should be jealous of his woman, and she herself should not have been defiled; and the human will lead his woman toward the priest, and he will bring forward the gift about her, the tenth of the ephah barley flour; he will not pour oil upon it, nor will he put frankincense upon it; for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, a sacrifice of memorial, reminding sin. And the priest will bring her near, and will stand her opposite Lord, and the priest will take clean living water in a clay vessel, and of the earth being upon the floor of the tent of the witness; and the priest having taken will cast into the water, and the priest will stand the woman opposite Lord, and will uncover the head of the woman, and will give upon her hands the sacrifice of the memorial, the sacrifice of the jealousy; and in the hand of the priest will be the water of the conviction of this having-been-cursed; and the priest will oath her, and will say to the woman: If someone has not slept with you, if you have not transgressed to be defiled under your own man, be guiltless from the water of the conviction of this having-been-cursed. And if you have transgressed being under-man, if you have been defiled, and someone has given his bed in you, yet of your man; and the priest will oath the woman in the oaths of this curse, and the priest will say to the woman: May Lord give you in a curse and an oath in midst of your people, in Lord’s giving your thigh having fallen-through, and your belly having been inflamed. And this cursing water will go into your belly, to inflame a stomach, and for your thigh to fall-through. And the woman will say: May it become, may it become. And the priest will write these curses into a book, and will wipe-out into the water of the conviction of the having-been-cursed, and will make the woman drink the water of the conviction of the having-been-cursed. And the cursing water of the conviction will go into her; and the priest will take from hand of the woman the sacrifice of the jealousy, and will put the sacrifice opposite Lord, and will bring it forward toward the altar. And the priest will grasp from the sacrifice its memorial, and it will be brought-up upon the altar, and after these he will make the woman drink the water. And it will be, if she should be defiled and should escape-escape her man, and the cursing water of the conviction will go into her, and she will be inflamed as to the belly, and her thigh will fall-through, and the woman will be unto a curse for her people. And if she should not be defiled’
translator_notes: Ends mid μὴ μιανθῇ into §14 ἡ γυνή; single long Cyril paragraph; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Ordeal types Christ’s judgment seat; barley vs wheat gift
english: Cyril: …the woman, and she should be clean, and she will be guiltless, and she will seed-out seed.’ These things at least, the law. And I would say that having brought-together very well the about the having-been-written leisurely in few thoughts, the divine Paul writes for us: ‘For all us must be manifested before the tribunal of the Christ, in order that each may receive-back the through the body toward what he practiced either good things, or worthless.’
Palladius: I think these have been said rightly; yet clarify finely the upon each of the having-been-legislated.

Cyril: The woman in suspicions of having been adulterated, whenever she should endure a deserted writing of convicting, he has ordered to be led toward the priest, and indeed also to have stood in eyes of God, and this, I think, is the all about to be stood-beside for the Christ; then the gift being brought-near over her barley flour, not having been sprinkled-through with frankincense, not having been soaked with oil; for it is a sacrifice of jealousy, reminding sin. So then clear that as it were some smell of each one’s life goes-up toward God, for those having been relaxed unto the easy bringing-on the writing upon all the most outlandish things, and for those at least having been eager very best to live rightly, witnessing-upon the genuine. In this way we say, and very reasonably, of those not being in suspicions, the gifts have the fine-flour from wheats, with frankincense being present, and indeed also oil being poured-down. For there will altogether follow for the still human life, of which also a type would be the fine-flour from wheats, the needing to be reckoned in sweet-fragrance and cheerfulness beside at least the virtue-loving God. And of a bastard and cattle-fitting life a sign would become also very clear, the barley flour; for somehow more cattle-fitting, and not resembling a human very much, the unrestrained unto appetite, and the wishing to go unbridled unto outlandish pleasures. In this way barley flour, the woman being charged upon a bastard life, was bringing-near to God, without frankincense and oil, that is, of sweet-fragrance and cheerfulness; for it is a sacrifice reminding sin. And where a reminder of sin, how or from where would the cheerful be? For not in hope of crowns the one being judged, but in fear of justice and fire. And toward these at least, uncovered the woman is brought-near to the judge, that is, not in the customary and fitting adornment. And what word would there be of this? For of disorder the charges, and of abomination the writing. And remember that an uncovered woman he does not allow to pray to God, Paul being law-learned, having taken the needing for her to be covered-down the law of the nature unto a showing. ‘For the hair,’ he says, ‘instead of a wrap-around has been given to her.’ So then no longer was the little-woman in adornment, having been slandered upon disorder. And uncovered also otherwise; for bare in eyes of the judging one are the all things, and no one at all would escape the one searching hearts and kidneys, and through a prophet’s voice saying thus: ‘A God drawing-near I am, says Lord, and not a God from far. Will something be hidden from me?’ Yet that Christ is the judging one, he under-shows again riddlingly. For water, he said, both living and clean’
translator_notes: Ends mid καθαρὸν into §15 εἰς ἀγγεῖον; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Living water in clay = Word in flesh; curse words = cross; virtue twofold
english: Cyril: …must be put into a clay vessel, and indeed also from the earth being upon the tent. Then with the words of the curse having been washed-in in water, he ordered the woman in suspicions of having been whored to drink. And, ‘If on the one hand she should be liable to the charge, she will be inflamed,’ he says, ‘as to a belly, and a thigh will fall; and if on the other she has been freed of the cause, and not true upon her the having-been-supposed, she will seed-out seed.’
Palladius: So then what the word? or how would also through the just now having-been-named, the Christ be signaled for us?

Cyril: For through the living and clean water, you will understand the life-making the Word of God, the truly clean, and altogether without-share of sin, who has become in flesh, just as in a clay vessel. For that dust also and from earth the flesh, how or from where doubtful? And through at least the earth from the tent, you will think the in death through us; for it has been said to the nature of human: ‘Earth you are, and unto earth you will go away.’ And through at least the words of the curse, you will understand very well the having become a curse over us, through the having been hung upon wood. For it has been written, that also ‘Cursed every one hanging upon wood.’ So then whenever into the depth of the human mind Emmanuel being God according to nature should arrive, those liable to faults, he will convict punishing; and those having been caught not in these, he will show-out fruit-bearing. For this, I think, is the, she will seed-out seed, the fruit-bearing of the soul, with the bodily passion signaling.
Palladius: You spoke most excellently.

Cyril: So then fornication and the passions of flesh counterfeit the human, and stand-out from the familiarity toward God; for those being in flesh are not able to please God. And flesh, as I at least think, names the fleshly mindset. For thus the having-been-written would be thought rightly. And again a manner toward this worthlessness, and indeed also a rhythm of wildness of customs, and an going-out unto every whatever of the most outlandish, finishes us abominable and unholy. For it is not fitting for us to man-up only against fleshly passions, but also to shine-through with gentleness of customs, and to appear caretakers of love as much as most the unto brothers, and to be seen crowned with the boasts of justice, and toward these at least, to have a fine and practiced mind at least in themselves, striking-toward undistortedly the opinions about God, and in searches of doctrines everywhere saving the having blamelessly; for perfect such ones, according to the true being lacking of none of the best things; for the human of God must be complete also the divine Paul said for us; and ‘complete’ he says the having been fitted-out unto every good work, and having fittingly toward being able very well to set-upright the virtue. Or does it not hold thus?
Palladius: For how not?
Cyril: So then see how riddlingly the law unto
translator_notes: Ends mid εἰς into §16 ἀνθρωπίνων ἠθῶν; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Clean/unclean beasts type manners; chew cud and split hoof
english: Cyril: …a under-forming of human customs, having brought-beside both many animals of the irrational ones, and indeed also kinds of winged and water-ones, benefits us according to countless manners. And do not wonder at all, where also to plants themselves sometimes he likens, from each one’s natural quality signaling urbanely the upon each of the according to us. For somewhere God said through Isaiah’s voice, under-showing the sweet-fragrances of those having bloomed-up unto life unto Christ through faith, clear that the spiritual, and indeed also heights the unto virtue: ‘And I will make in the desert living water, and in waterless land rivers, and I will set unto the waterless land, cedar, and box, and myrtle, and cypress, and white-poplar.’ And again: ‘And it will be,’ he says, ‘instead of the brushwood, a cypress will go up; and instead of fleabane, a myrtle will go up;’ brushwood, I think somehow, and fleabane, naming well-naturedly the still untamed souls, and appearing in a form of the wild thorn beside at least the eyes of the divinity. But also to stones sometimes the reverend band of the holy ones is likened; ‘For holy stones are rolled upon the earth.’ And indeed also the kingdom of the heavens the Savior was saying to have resembled leaven and a grain of mustard. So then from many and most vivid examples the God-breathed Writing is accustomed to make-clear the human things.
Palladius: I agree.

Cyril: So then observe that having brought-beside usefully countless as many kinds of cattle, and indeed the of winged and the swimming, some, as unclean it defiles altogether, and others again it both accepts and frees of slander, in order that those serving God may know rightly, doing which things, they would not be received-in; and from which having held-off thoughtfully, they will be far of blame, and would be bright and acceptable, and having been honored with the vote from above. And the law upon this holds for us thus: ‘And Lord spoke toward Moses and Aaron, saying: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: These the cattle which you will eat from all the cattle the upon the earth, every cattle splitting a hoof, and clawing clawers of two hoofs, and bringing-up rumination in the cattle, these you will eat; yet from these you will not eat, from those bringing-up rumination, and from those splitting the hoofs, and clawing clawers; the camel, because it brings-up rumination, and a hoof it does not split, unclean this for you, and the rough-foot, because it brings-up rumination and a hoof it does not split, unclean this for you, and the porcupine, because it brings-up rumination, and a hoof it does not split, unclean this for you, and the swine, because it splits a hoof, this also claws nails of a hoof, and this does not bring-up rumination, unclean this for you. From their fleshes you will not eat, and of their carcasses you will not eat, unclean these for you.’ So then most vividly the Christ, ‘Not the going-into unto the mouth,’ he says, ‘commons the human.’ And it has been said somehow also toward the all-divine Peter, with the linen having been let-down from above by four beginnings, in which all have been written the’
translator_notes: Ends mid τὰ into §17 τετράποδα; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Peter’s sheet; beasts name manners; justice twofold self/others
english: Cyril: …four-foots and winged ones: ‘Having stood up Peter, sacrifice and eat.’ And with the disciple having cried-up and still fearing the legal watch, and saying, ‘Least, Lord, because I have never eaten every common or unclean, nor has every profane flesh gone into my mouth,’ again God was sounding: ‘What God has cleansed, you do not common.’ And also the all-divine Paul writes, that ‘Food does not stand us beside God.’ So then it is not unclear, that least does the law profane some of the beings, and it knows all clean for the clean; but having taken very well the natural of each animal unto qualities of human customs, it benefits not moderately. And you may learn what I say at least, also from these again, true that and undoubted. For the things having been condemned by all, it is seen having ordered needing to abominate, saying camel at least, and the porcupine, night-raven, and the diver, and lizard, and shrew-mouse, and the still more shameful than these. So then would not the aim of the lawgiver be vivid as at least in these, O good one?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: So then unto a quality of customs must be carried-over very well the things being naturally in some of the irrational animals, each, come say, as it were writing-down in itself the manner of so-and-so, and signaling in what things it would be. Or do not even we ourselves somehow custom to call those very hot and most well-strong, and exceeding the others in boldness, swine, or lions, or some other of such? and the meek and quiet, and having a lowered mind, sheep, and doves, and sometimes also to crown with the name of calm, bringing-on for each’s manners the fitting clarifying from the more apparent?
Palladius: True.
Cyril: So then let us go upon the aim of the law, and what ever it is which it enjoins, let us busy very well.
Palladius: Let us go.

Cyril: The boasts of justice, and simply of every fairness, go-forward on the one hand from each one’s judgment somehow, yet are set-upright according to a double manner, I think, and somehow have upon themselves a twofold showing-out.
Palladius: And how do you say?

Cyril: For either unto ourselves we do some of the good things, cutting-off the outlandish and blamed pleasures, deadening the members the upon the earth, setting the mind unto meekness the in spirit, practicing poverty, having the mind clean and unmuddied, as much as possible, or filling the good eager-acts unto brothers, gifting unhurtfulness to those having chosen to grieve and having struck-against unlovingly, helping the weary, encouraging having-been-grieved, turning-over unto the straight those having wandered from unlearning, hand-leading upon the better,
translator_notes: Ends mid χειραγωγοῦντες ἐπὶ τὸ ἄμεινον into §18 ἐπαρκοῦντες; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Split hoof = walk both ways; cud = ponder doctrines
english: Cyril: …sufficing for those needing, and having been very eager to finish-out very well the things upon which God would be gladdened. So then is not somehow twofold the manner of the justice, unto both ourselves, and indeed also unto others being set-upright?
Palladius: It seems so.

Cyril: So then with a split hoof, or a cloven of a foot, the law somehow always likens such a one. For a foot always would be a symbol and type for us of the practical journey according to energy; and indeed we say, to dart-through with a straight foot, those being very eager to go blamelessly toward the finishing unto benefit. And somewhere also David sings-up: ‘For my foot stood in straightness,’ that is, I have walked in justice and straightness; and I have hated the having-been-twisted. And about at least the sin-loving ones: ‘Sharp their feet to pour-out blood, and crushing and misery in their ways.’ So then of the journey in works a symbol the foot. And a cloven at least would be a clear type of our being able to walk upon both rightly and unrebukably, unto the according to ourselves, and indeed also unto others.
Palladius: Persuasive the word.

Cyril: So then if somehow there should be someone, knowing to walk upon both rightly and knowledgeably, able to benefit both himself and others, I say by the quality of the customs, and toward this at least, thoughtful and most prudent, and giving the heart as it were some lodging and dwelling for the words about God, always somehow turning up and down in himself the thoughts of the divine doctrines, and through this densely and prudently to search-out, thinning-down somehow the thus of the thoughts having been known accurately, he will altogether somehow have resembled an animal bringing-up the chewing, and always belching-up the nourishment in a belly, and leading-under to the teeth, in order that it may also still be ground-fine, and by the thin of the digestion may go toward benefit.
Palladius: You speak well.

Cyril: And he says the animal is clean, which ever should have the foot finishing toward a splitting hoof, and again bring-back the chewing in a belly; for the one having been naturally both excellent and good unto himself and others, and having taken-on also the word-loving and the practiced unto knowledge, clear that the upon God, will be complete toward virtue, and having blamelessly at least in the according to himself, toward every whatever of the having-been-wondered; and if somehow someone should become a sharer of such, I say according to learning, and as it were somehow feast-down the word from him, and if he should become an imitator, and should choose to zeal the thus distinguished and exceptional, he will be unprofane and clean. For he will live-with a clean one, and will show-out at once his own manner as it were some impress of the understanding and good-learning in him. This, I think, is the needing for us to eat from every animal naturally splitting the foot into a hoof, and bringing-up’
translator_notes: Ends mid ἀνάγοντος into §19 μηρυκισμόν; PG mid-cut kept.

title: Cud without hoof / hoof without cud incomplete; heretic leftovers
english: Cyril: …rumination. For such the law says clean, according at least to the word just having become.
Palladius: I have understood what you say.

Cyril: So then the excellent and having completely toward virtue, he under-showed riddlingly, as at least in an animal, the one having been natural to split, and bringing-up rumination. And that beautiful and benefit-bearing to love to shake-off the one not having judgment thus, and as it were limping toward the good, and going behind of completeness the unto virtue, he enjoins again, neither for those bringing-up rumination, without having obtained the splitting, nor indeed for those having been natural to split, if they should not have rumination, having brought-on the best vote, and rather writing-down their unclean, and setting them numbered with those knowing to defile-down. So then of practical energy and quality of manners, the cloven of the foot, we affirm to be a type, thinking rightly, and reshaping the having-been-said riddlingly unto truth. And the rumination at least, we define to be a sign of word according to piety, and of dogmatic knowledge, both right and practiced. Or does it not hold thus?
Palladius: Very much so.

Cyril: So then incomplete toward virtue would reasonably be thought, and he has stood far of the needing to be wondered-at, the one boasting in good works, yet being worsted of the dogmatic rightness, and not having words of the truth unto mind. And true that also the reverse, not unclear; for dogmatic rightness, and the sweet care of the divine words, would benefit us nothing, unto at least the having completely unto a reputation of virtue, with the brightness in works not having been yoked-beside. For the one right upon both, will carry-away the vote of the being well-reputed completely. And the one lacking of the other, will have strengthless the being wondered-at in the beautiful. Some such also the Savior under-shows, saying, least in the kingdom of the heavens to have been called the one teaching on the one hand, yet not still also having done; and great again and distinguished, the one having practiced and having taught. So then unclean according to law, the one being worsted of one. And that it is fitting to depart from these, and according to no manner to be seen having shared, he was clarifying saying: ‘From the fleshes you will not eat, and of their carcasses you will not touch.’ For neither with living ones, he says, will you be turned-about-with. And if somehow one of such should have died, you will keep your own mind unprofane; not even so much as to say touching of the things having been made by those, clear that of words, and of polluted compositions; for such are leftovers of a human’s life. This at least the unlearned heretics are accustomed to do. For they have wandered admittedly, the ones having become teachers of the unlearning being in them; and leftovers as it were of their own impiety they have deposited-beside for their own disciples; and they, also very gladly both accept and house-in according to mind, and have a hard-to-wash-out defilement, touching as it were carcass fleshes, which are full of the last foul-smell and uncleanness.
translator_notes: Book 14 mid; heretic leftovers typology.

title: Camel/hare/pig types; works without piety dead; water-creatures begin
english: Palladius: True.

Cyril: So then he receives unto an example of the not splitting on the one hand the hoof, yet bringing-back the rumination, the camel, an animal both well-strong and over-great, and rough-foot and porcupine, the most small-appearing as a word to say of all the others, through the extremes, as I at least think, having embraced all together, and having released nothing outside of the through the middle. For like as if somehow it should also be said, From the very high and uppermost and until small ones, and of the as much as most lowest, every who at least such is abominable and unclean. For there is not face-taking beside God, according to the having-been-written; but whether someone should be great and haughty, having been lifted unto height with wealth and glory the according to world, he will carry-away the unfamed and unprized vote, being held in the charges of worthlessness; or whether someone should be small, living-with poverty and unglory, he will be condemned toward uncleanness, if he should not boast in the manners unto virtue; nor would someone make a find of the lowliness, the needing to be pitied beside the just Judge, not having the well-fitting in works, clear that the according to piety and virtue. So then a camel on the one hand, and a hare and a porcupine, would be a not unclear type of small and great. And he also brings-beside the swine, as unclean, through at least the splitting on the one hand a hoof, yet not still also having been natural also to chew-up nourishment, that is, to bring-up rumination, showing strengthless and useless the boast in works, without the word the according to piety. For just as the faith without the works is dead, so also the reverse, somehow altogether dead the good-order, and the fair in works, with God-knowledge being absent, and with word the according to piety not having house-dwelt in our souls, and being below, it has nodded-in unto earth, and somehow seems to fear the raising-up above the eye. Some such having suffered we will find not few, who sometimes have a reverend and clean life, yet not having recognized God the by nature and true, as it were somehow only fix the eye of the mind upon the upon the earth. And unclean also such again; ‘For no one is crowned, if he should not contend lawfully,’ according to the having-been-written.
Palladius: So then it defiles us as in a form of a swine, and indeed also of the others, those having been borne-under the slanders from law.

Cyril: Very much so you spoke rightly. And it is not sufficient for the law to bring-beside the images of the unclean, and through at least only also of such somehow, but through as it were all the creation having chosen to benefit us and setting-beside richly the knowledge of the useful and fitting, it also goes-through the kinds of water-ones, and herds of winged ones, in order that busying very well the having grown for each, what on the one hand thereafter would be the pleasing God, and what rejectable and having been hated by him we may have to think-around
translator_notes: Ends mid περινοεῖν ἔχοιμε into later §§; tip §§11–20.
